editorial.headline: Private Vocational Schools: Nationally Open, Unblocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Private secondary vocational education is open to full foreign ownership nationally, and Bali does not place it within its PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
Private secondary vocational education is an institutional activity, centred on a privately organised vocational high school rather than on a single trade. It includes private vocational schools and private special schools at the secondary level for students with special educational needs. The curriculum may range across tourism, culinary arts, management, office work, hospitality, engineering, pharmacy, beauty and hair, and agriculture. The scope also expressly includes a vocational school formed through cooperation with a foreign education institution, provided that institution is accredited or recognised in its own country and works with an Indonesian education institution on the formal education pathway. It remains a secondary education category, with vocational study delivered in a school setting. The common thread is the private delivery and management of secondary vocational schooling, whether the programme has a conventional specialist focus or is shaped through formal international educational collaboration.

The entity described here is the private party that organises or manages the vocational-school unit. That can include a private provider operating an ordinary vocational secondary school, a private special school at that level, or an Indonesian education institution involved in the specified formal cooperation. The listed scale range is broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open to the activity. The scale entries establish the coverage available in the record, from Mikro through Besar without narrowing it to a particular school subject. Nationally, the foreign-investment position is clear. The activity is open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%. In practical terms, the national ceiling permits full foreign ownership; it is not a partial-equity category. This national position is the starting point for assessing the Bali position.

Bali does not reverse that national position. The provincial moratorium is permanent and island-wide, and it blocks PMA registration for activities classified Low or Medium-Low risk. Yet this activity is not marked as blocked in Bali. The Bali record places its OSS risk at the Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range—Medium-High/High—and expressly says that it is not blocked by the moratorium. The result is a clean but important distinction: Bali’s restriction exists, but its stated trigger does not catch this activity. A foreign investor is therefore not barred from PMA registration in Bali by that moratorium, while the national ownership ceiling remains 100%. The Bali status is recorded as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, an affirmative position that still reflects the stated risk description at the Besar scale.
